results.summary: This is a minimal digital circuit created as a first ASIC design in a Tiny Tapeout and UCSD class starting November 2024. The documentation does not describe the logic function or how the four inputs map to the two outputs. Testing is listed as to-be-determined, with a logic analyzer suggested as helpful external hardware. The project is notable mainly as a beginner class exercise rather than for any specific circuit capability.

This design implements a switch-combination puzzle where the correct pattern of inputs turns on a light output. Inputs pass through directly, through an OR gate, and through a NOT gate to produce the outputs, and the user experiments with switch settings to find the winning combination. It needs an LED and a 7-segment display as external hardware. The documentation is thin and does not state the exact winning combination or the full truth table.

This design takes two 2-bit numbers A and B and a 4-bit number C from eight input pins, computes A times B plus C, and displays the result on a 7-segment display. The decimal point indicates an offset of 16, so a displayed digit plus 16 gives the true value. It requires no external hardware beyond the display, and the documentation gives a worked example of 3 times 3 plus 15 equals 24. The design is a compact arithmetic and display exercise built in Wokwi.

This design outputs a counter on the output and bidirectional pins when a select signal is high, and mirrors the bidirectional pins to the outputs when select is low. Testing consists of setting select high to observe the counter and low to observe the mirroring behavior. No external hardware is required. The documentation is minimal and the project appears to be a basic Tiny Tapeout template or introductory exercise.

This project is a guessing game in which the user tries to find an input combination that makes the displayed number zero. Inputs 0 through 7 feed a mix of AND and XOR logic that drives LED and display outputs. A 7-segment display is the only external hardware needed. The documentation is vague about the exact logic and winning combination, so the precise behavior cannot be fully determined from the text.

This is a one-bit half adder that computes sum as A XOR B and carry as A AND B from two input pins. The truth table is documented and the design is tested by connecting LEDs to the sum and carry outputs and observing them for each input combination. Two LED bulbs are the only external hardware required. It is a straightforward educational logic design demonstrating basic arithmetic at the gate level.

This project is described as an encoder design, though the one-line description calls it an 8x3 decoder. The documentation gives no logic table, pin mapping, or functional detail beyond the instruction to toggle the design. No external hardware is listed. The documentation is too thin to determine the actual function or how it should be tested.

This design is an active-high 7-to-3 encoder with an option to invert its outputs, documented with a gate diagram and truth table. Seven input lines are toggled and the first three output lines are connected to LEDs to observe the binary representation of the active input. A TTBoard and LEDs are sufficient external hardware. It is a clear introductory logic project with a 1 Hz clock specified.

This design maps input combinations to letters shown on a display, for example input 0 alone shows A and input 1 alone shows B. The documentation describes the general idea of displaying corresponding letters but does not give a complete mapping or truth table. A 7-segment display is the required external hardware. The project is an educational character-decoding exercise with incomplete documentation.

This project implements an adder circuit using XOR, AND, and OR gates on its input pins. The documentation states only that it performs addition of numbers and suggests using seven switches to test it. A 7-segment display is listed as external hardware. The description is too brief to determine the exact bit width or output encoding of the adder.
